{{short description|Depiction of mathematical topics on postage stamps}}
[[File:450th birth anniversary of Copernicus Poland 1923.jpg|thumb|[[Nicolaus Copernicus]], Poland, 1923|150px]]
[[File:Franklin SC1 1847.jpg|thumb|[[Benjamin Franklin]], USA, 1847|150px]]
[[File:DR 1926 395 Gottfried Wilhelm Leibniz.jpg|thumb|[[Gottfried Wilhelm Leibniz]], Germany, 1926|150px]]
The depiction of '''mathematics on stamps''' began in 1923 with the issue of a set of three Polish stamps commemorating the 450th birth anniversary of the astronomer and mathematician [[Nicolaus Copernicus]]. As the definition of what constitutes a valid mathematical stamp is not universally agreed, some collectors make the case that the first mathematical stamp was the 1847 United States issue depicting the polymath [[Benjamin Franklin]] even though he was not primarily a mathematician;<ref name=Wilson1>{{cite book
| last1 = Wilson
| first1 = Robin J.
| title = Stamping through mathematics
| publisher = Springer
| date = 2001
| location = New York
| pages = 144
| url = https://archive.org/details/stampingthroughm0000wils
| isbn = 978-0-387-98949-5
| doi = 10.1007/b97482
}}</ref>{{rp|64}} others prefer to recognize the 1926 German [[Leibniz]] stamp as the first depicting a mathematician.<ref>{{cite journal
| last1 = Brooke
| first1 = Maxey
| title = Mathematics and philately
| journal = Mathematics Magazine
| volume = 34
| number = 1
| date = 1960
| publisher =
| location =
| pages = 31-32
| doi = 10.2307/2687845
}}</ref>

The total number of mathematical stamps that have been issued is approximately 1,600 as of 2024.<ref name=Wilson3>{{cite journal
| last1 = Wilson
| first1 = Robin J.
| title = My favorite mathematical stamps: 40 years of ''Intelligencer'' Stamp Corners
| journal = The Mathematical Intelligencer
| volume = 46
| number = 1
| date = 2024
| publisher = Springer
| location = New York
| pages = 70–77
| doi = 10.1007/s00283-023-10305-2
}}</ref><ref>{{cite web
| title = Jeff Miller's postage stamps
| date = 2021
| publisher = [[MacTutor History of Mathematics Archive]] at the [[University of St Andrews]]
| url = https://mathshistory.st-andrews.ac.uk/Miller/stamps/
}}</ref>

==Definition==
A mathematical stamp has one or more of the following characteristics:
* It depicts a [[mathematician]], or a [[polymath]] with a significant mathematical output<ref>{{cite journal
| last1 = Boyer
| first1 = Carl B.
| title = Mathematics and philately
| journal = Scripta Mathematica
| volume = 15
| number =
| date = 1949
| publisher =
| location =
| pages = 105-114}}</ref>
* It depicts a [[mathematical concept]] or [[mathematical object]]
* It depicts a [[mathematical symbol]], [[formula]] or [[Mathematical notation|notation]]
* It commemorates a mathematical event such as a national or [[International Congress of Mathematicians|international congress]], or an [[International Mathematical Olympiad]]
* It depicts the process of [[mathematics education]],<ref name=Wilson1/>{{rp|v}} or a building used primarily for mathematical research or education

Stamps illustrating [[applied mathematics]] such as [[astronomy]], [[ballistics]], [[cartography]], [[crystallography]], [[Mathematics and art|mathematical art]], [[Recreational mathematics|mathematical games]], [[navigation]], [[Perspective (graphical)|perspective in art]] and [[spaceflight]] may or may not be included in a mathematical stamp collection depending on the breadth of view of the collector. Typically such stamps may depict a mathematically related object or instrument, e.g. an [[astrolabe]] or a [[slide rule]].

The following types of material are excluded (although they may also be collected by mathematical stamp enthusiasts):
* [[Postal stationery]],<ref>{{cite web |title=Postal stationery offers collecting variety |url=https://www.linns.com/news/postal-updates-page/stamp-collecting-basics/2002/january/postal-stationery-offers-collecting-variety-.html |first=Rick |last=Miller |publisher=[[Linns Stamp News]] |date=14 January 2012 |access-date=8 May 2024}}</ref> e.g. a postcard depicting a mathematician with a non-mathematical stamp affixed
* [[Cinderella stamp|Cinderella]], [[Local post|local]], private or personal issues, i.e. unofficial stamps
* Non-postal stamps, e.g. [[revenue stamp]]s<ref>{{cite book|title=Philatelic Terms Illustrated |last1=Mackay |first1=James |edition=4th |publisher=Stanley Gibbons Limited |date=2003 |pages=170 |isbn=9780852595572}}</ref>
* Stamps issued by non-existing/unrecognized countries and/or in excess of actual postal requirements

Stamps depicting individual mathematicians are often issued by countries to commemorate the birth or death anniversaries of their significant national mathematicians, for example stamps issued by Norway celebrating [[Niels Henrik Abel]].<ref name=Larsen1>{{cite journal
| last1 = Larsen
| first1 = H.D.
| title = Historically speaking - Mathematics on stamps
| journal = The Mathematics Teacher
| volume = 48
| number = 7
| date = 1955
| publisher = National Council of Teachers of Mathematics
| location =
| pages = 477-480
| doi = 10.5951/MT.48.7.0477
| jstor = 27954992
}}</ref><ref name=Larsen2>{{cite journal
| last1 = Larsen
| first1 = H.D.
| title = Historically speaking - Mathematics on stamps
| journal = The Mathematics Teacher
| volume = 49
| number = 5
| date = 1956
| publisher = National Council of Teachers of Mathematics
| location =
| pages = 395-396
| doi = 10.5951/MT.49.5.0395
| jstor =
}}</ref> Examples are illustrated in the gallery above. Some countries have also issued stamps depicting internationally famous mathematicians such as [[Isaac Newton]]<ref>{{cite journal
| last1 = Smorynski
| first1 = Craig
| title = North Korea's Newton stamps with a checklist of all Newton stamps known to man
| journal = Philamat
| volume = 21
| number = 4
| date = 2000
| publisher = Mathematical study unit of the American Topical Association
| location =
| pages = 6-12
| doi =
}}</ref> or [[Albert Einstein]].<ref>{{cite book|title=Albert Einstein on stamps: a catalog |last1=Raddi |first1=Albert |publisher=American Topical Association |location=Greer, SC |date=2020 |pages=168 |isbn=979-8663466219}}</ref>

===Mathematical concepts and objects===
<gallery mode=packed heights=160px style="text-align:left">
PythagoreanTheoremGreekStamp.jpg|[[Pythagorean theorem]], Greece, 1955
Stamp_of_Brazil_-_1967_-_Colnect_263101_-_Mobius_Symbol.jpeg|[[Möbius strip]], Brazil, 1967
DBP 1977 928 Carl Friedrich Gauß.jpg|[[Complex plane]], West Germany, 1977
Stamp Germany 1998 MiNr2005 Internationaler Mathematiker-Kongress.jpg|[[Squaring the square|Squaring a rectangle]], Germany, 1998
</gallery>
Stamps depicting a mathematical concept or object, sometimes combined with a portrait of the mathematician responsible for inventing the concept or object, are generally issued as [[commemorative stamp]]s rather than [[definitive stamp]]s. Examples are shown in the gallery above: a 1955 Greek stamp illustrating the [[Pythagorean theorem]], a 1967 Brazilian stamp illustrating a [[Möbius strip]] and also commemorating the 6th Brazilian mathematical congress, a 1977 West German stamp illustrating the [[complex plane]] and also commemorating the 200th birth anniversary of [[Carl Gauss]], and a 1998 German stamp illustrating [[Squaring the square|squaring a rectangle]] and also commemorating an International Mathematical Congress.

===Mathematical symbols and formulae===
<gallery mode=packed heights=130px style="text-align:left">
The Soviet Union 1966 CPA 3310 stamp (The International Congress of Mathematicians (ICM) (16-26.08, Moscow). Emblem - Integral Symbol and Globe. Sum and Union Symbols).jpg|[[International Congress of Mathematicians]], USSR, 1966
Luzinstamp.jpg|[[Nikolai Luzin]], Russia, 2000
Czech stamp 2000 m259.jpg|[[Fermat's Last Theorem]], Czech Republic, 2000
75th anniversary of Mathematical Society of Serbia 2023.jpg|[[Fibonacci sequence]], Serbia, 2023
</gallery>

Stamps depicting a mathematical symbol or formula are frequently depicted together with the mathematician they are primarily associated with.<ref>{{cite book |last1=Wussing |first1=Hans |editor1-last=Grattan-Guinness |editor1-first=Ivor |title=Companion Encyclopedia of the History and Philosophy of the Mathematical Sciences |date=1994 |volume=2 |publisher=Routledge |location=London |isbn=0-415-09239-6 |pages=1650–1658 |chapter=Stamping mathematics}}</ref> Examples are shown in the gallery above: a 1966 Soviet stamp illustrating the [[Integral symbol|integral]], [[summation]] and [[Union (set theory)|union]] symbols and also commemorating an International Mathematical Congress, a 2000 Russian stamp illustrating the [[pi]],<ref>{{cite journal
| last1 = Egelriede
| first1 = Dieter
| title = About the Number π
| journal = Philamat
| volume = 33
| number = 2
| date = 2011
| publisher = Mathematical study unit of the American Topical Association
| location =
| pages = 3-8
| doi =
}}</ref> [[Function (mathematics)|function]] and [[summation]] symbols and commemorating the life of [[Nikolai Luzin]], a 2000 Czech stamp illustrating [[Fermat's Last Theorem]] and commemorating [[Andrew Wiles]]'s 1995 proof, and a 2023 Serbian stamp illustrating the [[Fibonacci sequence]] and commemorating the 75th anniversary of the Mathematical Society of Serbia.

==Publications==
[[Robin Wilson (mathematician)|Robin J. Wilson]] is the leading writer in the field having published a well-reviewed<ref>{{cite journal
| last1 = Abbott
| first1 = Steve
| title = Stamping through mathematics (review)
| journal = The Mathematical Gazette
| volume = 86
| number = 507
| date = 2002
| pages = 549–550
| doi = 10.2307/3621187
}}</ref><ref>{{cite journal
| last1 = Russ
| first1 = Rebecca
| title = Stamping through mathematics (review)
| journal = Math Horizons
| volume = 11
| number = 16
| date = 2004
| pages = 29
| doi = 10.1080/10724117.2004.12021774
}}</ref><ref name=Hansen>{{cite journal
| last1 = Hansen
| first1 = V.L.
| title = Stamping through mathematics (review)
| journal = The Mathematical Intelligencer
| volume = 26
| number =
| date = 2004
| pages = 78
| doi = 10.1007/BF02985663
}}</ref> book entitled ''Stamping through mathematics'' in 2001,<ref name=Wilson1/> a paper on European mathematical history through stamps,<ref name=Wilson2>{{cite conference
| last1 = Wilson
| first1 = Robin J.
| title = European mathematics: a history in stamps
| book-title = European Congress of Mathematics
| date = 2023
| publisher = EMS Press
| location = Berlin
| pages = 677–691
| doi = 10.4171/8ECM/28
| isbn = 978-3-98547-051-8
| doi-access = free
}}</ref> and also contributing the Stamp Corner column to ''[[The Mathematical Intelligencer]]'' starting in 1984.<ref name=Wilson3/>

William L. Schaaf published a paper,<ref name=Schaaf1>{{cite journal
| last1 = Schaaf
| first1 = William L.
| title = Mathematics in use, as seen on postage stamps
| journal = The Mathematics Teacher
| volume = 67
| number = 1
| date = 1974
| publisher = The National Council of Teachers of Mathematics
| location = Reston, VA
| pages = 16–24
| doi = 10.5951/mt.67.1.0016
}}</ref> later expanded into a book entitled ''Mathematics and science: an adventure in postage stamps'' in 1978.<ref name=Schaaf2>{{cite book
| last1 = Schaaf
| first1 = William L.
| title = Mathematics and science: an adventure in postage stamps
| publisher = The National Council of Teachers of Mathematics
| location = Reston, VA
| date = 1978
| pages = 172
| url = https://archive.org/details/mathematicsscien0000scha
| isbn = 0-87353-122-1
}}</ref> From 1979 until at least 2011 the Mathematical Study Unit of the [[American Topical Association]] published ''Philamat: A journal of mathematical philately'' but this organization is no longer part of the ATA as of 2024. A sample issue is available online.<ref>{{cite web
| title = Philamat: A journal of mathematical philately, vol. 33, no. 2
| date = 2011
| publisher = Mathematical Study Unit of the American Topical Association
| pages = 1–12
| oclc = 730257354
| url = https://www.filatelista-tematico-blog.net/wp-content/uploads/Dia_do_pi_about_the_number_pi.pdf
}}</ref>

Listings of new issues of mathematical stamps are included in the monthly [[Scott catalogue|Scott]] Stamp magazine and in [[Linn's Stamp News]]; they are also available online from October 2010 to date in the Computers and Mathematics section.<ref>{{cite web
| title = Stamp programs: by topic
| date = July 2024
| publisher = Linn's Stamp News
| url = https://www.linns.com/insights/stamp-programs/listings-by-topic
}}</ref>
